text: Time to turn the plan from last lesson into real T-SQL. Everything here against AdventureWorks2012 -- nothing invented, just one hop deeper through the category hierarchy than a simpler report would need.

The FROM and JOIN block matches the plan exactly. Start at SalesOrderDetail, aliased sod. Join up to SalesOrderHeader, aliased soh, on SalesOrderID. Join sideways to Product, aliased p, on ProductID. Join up to ProductSubcategory, aliased psc, on ProductSubcategoryID. And join up once more to ProductCategory, aliased pc, on ProductCategoryID. Five tables, four join keys, same as the sketch.

The current-quarter filter builds its own date range instead of hardcoding one. DatePart quarter of GetDate gives today's quarter number, one through four. That gets converted into the quarter's starting month, and DateFromParts assembles day one of that month. The upper bound adds three months to that same date. The result is a half-open range -- on or after the quarter starts, strictly before the next one does -- so it never double-counts a boundary date, and it rolls forward automatically every quarter with zero edits.

The select list has one grouping column, the category name, plus sum of line total for total sales amount, and count distinct sales order id for order count. Group by category name matches that one non-aggregated column, exactly the GROUP BY rule you already know.

Here's a built-in sanity check worth knowing before you even run it: AdventureWorks2012 has exactly four product categories -- Bikes, Components, Clothing, and Accessories. So a correct run of this query can never return more than four rows. If it ever comes back with more than four, something upstream in the joins or the grouping is wrong.
That's a complete, correct extract query, ready to run against AdventureWorks2012. Next lesson, we bring its results into Power BI and start shaping them in Power Query.
